implementation_notes: Kotlin's sealed hierarchies close the state set and when over them is exhaustive, so the compiler rather than a runtime check reports an unhandled state; this replaces the Context/State class hierarchy. Two shapes are common: state objects (data object Draft : Phase) with behaviour methods and a context holding var phase: Phase, or a pure transition function using when (phase) that returns the successor. Sealed subclasses must live in the same package and module, which keeps the state set next to the context; fall back to an ordinary open hierarchy or an interface when third parties must add states.
code_sketch:
sealed interface Phase
data object Draft : Phase
data object Published : Phase

fun next(phase: Phase): Phase = when (phase) {
    Draft -> Published       // no else branch: the compiler checks exhaustiveness
    Published -> phase
}
pitfalls: Adding an else branch to silence the compiler removes the exhaustiveness check permanently.
Sealed subclasses are module-local, so plugin-provided states are impossible by construction - plan for an interface if that is required.
A var phase mutated from several coroutines races; confine transitions to one dispatcher or update it through MutableStateFlow.update.
